analysis.subject: chemistry
analysis.pageCoverage: page covers plutonium as a man-made radioactive element formed when uranium absorbs neutrons, its alpha emissions and isotopes with half-life examples, decay to daughter products, and uses in pacemakers, space missions and reactor fuel including spent fuel and reprocessing to MOX fuel

overview.headline: Plutonium isotopes, half life, decay and reactor fuel cycle

keyPoints.point: Students learn that plutonium is a radioactive metallic element with atomic number 94 created when uranium absorbs neutrons.
keyPoints.quote: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element with the atomic number 94.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that different plutonium isotopes have different half-lives defined as time to lose half of radioactivity.
keyPoints.quote: The different isotopes have different “half-lives” – the time it takes to lose half of its radioactivity.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that Pu-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years while Pu-241 has a half-life of 14.4 years and shorter half-lives decay more quickly.
keyPoints.quote: Pu-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years and Pu-241’s half-life is 14.4 years.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that spent nuclear fuel contains about 1 percent plutonium by weight and reprocessing separates it for mixed oxide fuel.
keyPoints.quote: Spent nuclear fuel from U.S. reactors contains about 1 percent plutonium by weight.

keyTerms.gloss: metallic radioactive element that is created in reactors when uranium atoms absorb neutrons
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element with the atomic number 94.

keyTerms.gloss: type of radiation easily stopped with short range emitted by plutonium
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium predominantly emits alpha particles – a type of radiation that is easily stopped and has a short range.

keyTerms.gloss: time it takes for half of the radioactivity of an isotope to decay
keyTerms.quote: The different isotopes have different “half-lives” – the time it takes to lose half of its radioactivity.

keyTerms.gloss: able to split apart when struck by a neutron
keyTerms.quote: These are all “fissionable” – the atom’s nucleus can easily split apart if it is struck by a neutron.

keyTerms.gloss: process that uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other products
keyTerms.quote: This process, known as reprocessing, uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products.
